body.hook: Musicians count all the time, even in their heads during rests. Counting out loud is how you train your brain to know exactly where every note starts and stops.

study.title: Count It Out
study.question: How does counting aloud help me play rhythms?
study.passage:
Counting chart (written for this lesson; 4/4 time):
Whole note: 4 beats: "1 2 3 4" (hold). Whole rest: a full bar of silence; it hangs below the fourth line.
Half note: 2 beats: "1 2." Half rest: sits on the third line, like a hat.
Quarter note: 1 beat: "1." Quarter rest: a squiggle.
Eighth notes: half a beat each, counted "1 &"; two eighths beamed together = 1 beat. Eighth rest: like a 7.
Steps: 1. Count each value while tapping the beat with your foot. 2. Clap and count four-bar rhythms from the board (e.g. | ♩ ♩ 𝅗𝅥 | ♫ ♫ ♩ ♩ | 𝅝 | ♩ rest ♫ ♩ |). 3. Whisper the counts during rests, and keep the foot tapping. 4. Partner game: one writes a one-bar rhythm, the other counts and claps it.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.

study.title: Rhythm Meets Pitch
study.question: How do I play rhythms accurately on my instrument?
study.passage:
Rhythm-on-pitch routine (written for this lesson; percussion plays on pad or mallets):
1. Clap and count first (always).
2. Play on one note: rhythms from the last lesson on Concert B♭ at 72 BPM.
3. Change notes: | B♭ B♭ C C | D D E♭ E♭ | F (whole) | F E♭ D C | B♭ (whole) | (quarter notes on concert pitches).
4. Add eighths: | B♭ & C & D & E♭ & | F (half) F (half) |.
5. Full value: hold half and whole notes to the very end of their beats. Count in your head "1-2-3-4" while holding.
6. Repeat sign: play the 4-bar line, then repeat from the start.
7. Play with a metronome, then without; did you stay steady?
Checklist: count first, check key signature (none yet, just the concert notes), tongue each note, keep air flowing, hold full value.

body.objective: Students will be able to sight-read a short line.
body.iCan: I can sight-read a short line.
successCriteria: I can use a checklist to prepare to sight-read
I can keep going even if I make a mistake
I can sight-read a short line accurately
body.hook: In auditions and concerts, musicians sometimes get music they've never seen and must play it right away. That skill, sight-reading, gets easier when you have a plan for the 30 seconds before you start.

vocabulary.definition: Playing music the first time you see it.
Sharps or flats at the start of a line that apply to the whole piece.

study.title: First Look
study.question: How can I play music I've never seen before?
study.passage:
Sight-reading checklist (written for this lesson), "STARS":
S: Signatures: key signature (sharps or flats) and time signature.
T: Tempo: marking and speed; choose a speed you can manage.
A: Accidentals and articulations: any extra sharps, flats or naturals, and markings like accents.
R: Rhythms: find the hardest bar and count it.
S: Signs: repeats, dynamics, first and second endings.
Routine: 30 seconds to scan with STARS, then silently finger through, then play. Rule: keep going; if you miss a note, jump back in on the next beat.
Practice: three 4-bar lines on the five concert notes, getting gradually harder (line 1: quarters and halves; line 2: adds eighths and rests; line 3: adds a repeat and dynamics). Partner tracks how many bars were correct and whether you kept going.

discussion: Which part of STARS helped most?

study.product: Sight-read a new four-bar line using STARS and keep going to the end; record bars correct and one thing to improve.
